title: History: what a source can and cannot establish

nodes.title: Provenance frames a source
nodes.summary: The author, date, location, and audience of a historical document help establish the conditions in which it was produced.

nodes.title: Purpose shapes a claim
nodes.summary: A document's intended audience and purpose can influence which events it describes and how it presents them.

nodes.title: Match the claim to the evidence
nodes.summary: A document that asserts a crowd's motives directly evidences the author's assertion, but does not by itself establish every participant's motive.

nodes.title: Independent corroboration
nodes.summary: Independent sources can strengthen a historical inference when they support it through distinct access to the events.

nodes.title: Repeated reports can share one origin
nodes.summary: Two newspapers copying the same report are not two independent eyewitness accounts.

nodes.title: Bias can itself be evidence
nodes.summary: A partisan source can provide evidence of its author's framing while requiring caution about the events or motives it describes.

messages.content: That makes sense. Let's work through the example, and please check where my intuition goes wrong.

content.text:
### A fictional source exercise
Imagine a fictional diplomatic letter reporting unrest and a fictional newspaper copying it. Neither text below is an archival quotation. Their agreement is not independent confirmation because both descend from one report. Compare with a separately produced account, asking what each observer could see.

For real documents to analyse, use [The National Archives' 1789 source collection](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/teaching-resources/french-revolution/).

### Provenance frames a source
The author, date, location, and audience of a historical document help establish the conditions in which it was produced.

### Purpose shapes a claim
A document's intended audience and purpose can influence which events it describes and how it presents them.

### Match the claim to the evidence
A document that asserts a crowd's motives directly evidences the author's assertion, but does not by itself establish every participant's motive.

arguments.explanation: Trace the reports' origins before counting independent support.

messages.content: If a source takes sides, isn't every sentence worthless?

content.text:
Reliability depends on the question. A partisan document may poorly establish an opponent's motives but strongly reveal its own rhetoric, intended audience, or political priorities. Support each inference with the right evidence and acknowledge uncertainty.

### Independent corroboration
Independent sources can strengthen a historical inference when they support it through distinct access to the events.

### Repeated reports can share one origin
Two newspapers copying the same report are not two independent eyewitness accounts.

### Bias can itself be evidence
A partisan source can provide evidence of its author's framing while requiring caution about the events or motives it describes.

arguments.question: What can a partisan pamphlet most directly show?

options.label: How its author presented an issue to an audience

arguments.explanation: Its framing is evidence even when its claims need corroboration.
